title: SRE Handbook: SLOs, Alerting and Incident Response
summary: Quick revision notes on defining reliability with SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, alerting on burn rate and symptoms, and running on-call, incidents and blameless postmortems.

chapters.title: SLIs, SLOs and SLAs: The Mental Model
points: SLI = measured ratio of good events to valid events, e.g. successful requests / total requests over a window
SLO = target for an SLI over a window, e.g. 99.9% of requests succeed over 30 days
SLA = contractual promise with penalties; set looser than the internal SLO
Pick SLIs from what users feel: availability, latency (percentile such as p99, not average), correctness, freshness
100% is the wrong target: cost rises steeply per extra nine and users cannot perceive it beyond their own network reliability

chapters.title: Error Budgets and Burn Rate
points: Error budget = 1 − SLO; a 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of downtime
Budget is spent by incidents, risky releases and planned maintenance; track remaining budget on a dashboard
Budget policy: if exhausted, freeze feature releases and prioritise reliability work until it recovers
Burn rate = observed error rate ÷ allowed error rate; 1 means budget lasts exactly the window, 14.4 means 2% of a 30-day budget gone in 1 hour
Use leftover budget deliberately for launches, experiments and chaos tests

chapters.title: Alerting on Symptoms, Not Causes
points: Page on user-visible symptoms (error rate, latency, SLO burn); causes like high CPU or a full disk go to dashboards or tickets
Multi-window burn-rate alerts: page at 14.4x over 1h confirmed by 5m; page at 6x over 6h confirmed by 30m; ticket at 1x over 3d
Short confirming window makes the alert reset quickly once the problem is fixed, avoiding stale pages
Every page must be urgent, actionable and need a human; otherwise delete it or downgrade to a ticket
Threshold alerts on raw metrics cause alert fatigue; alert on SLO consumption instead, e.g. Prometheus expression on error ratio > 14.4 * 0.001

chapters.title: On-Call and Runbooks
points: Healthy rotation: primary plus secondary, handoff notes, follow-the-sun if possible, and no more than about 2 pages per shift
Every alert links to a runbook: what it means, impact, how to verify, mitigation steps, escalation contact
Runbook steps should be copy-pasteable commands, e.g. kubectl rollout undo deploy/api, and tested during game days
Mitigate first, root-cause later: rollback, failover or feature-flag off beats debugging live
Track toil and page load per engineer; fix recurring pages or automate the runbook step

chapters.title: Incident Response and Blameless Postmortems
points: Incident roles: Incident Commander (decides and coordinates, does not debug), Ops lead (hands on fix), Communications lead (status page and stakeholders), Scribe (timeline)
Declare early with a severity level (SEV1-SEV3); severity drives who is paged and update cadence, e.g. every 30 minutes for SEV1
Keep one incident channel and a running timeline; hand over the IC role explicitly by saying so
Blameless postmortem: focus on system and process failures, not individuals; ask how the system allowed the mistake
Postmortem contents: impact, timeline, root causes and contributing factors, what went well, action items with owner and due date, reviewed within about 5 days

chapters.title: SRE Reliability Cheat Sheet
points: Error budget = 1 − SLO; 99.9% per 30d ≈ 43 min, 99.99% ≈ 4.3 min, 99% ≈ 7.2 h
Burn rate = error rate ÷ (1 − SLO); fast page 14.4x/1h+5m, slow page 6x/6h+30m, ticket 1x/3d
Page on symptoms, ticket on causes; every page needs a runbook link and a human action
IC coordinates, Ops fixes, Comms updates, Scribe records; mitigate before root cause
Postmortem: blameless, timeline, contributing factors, owned action items with deadlines
